summary: Fiscal Year 2026 Improper Payments The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) is committed to being a responsible steward of public funds and promoting the sustainability of its programs for future generations. Measuring improper payments is an important part of that responsibility. An improper payment is a payment that does not meet CMS program requirements. Improper payments include overpayments, underpayments, and payments for which there is insufficient information to determine whether payment requirements were met. Improper payment rates do not measure fraud. While some improper payments may involve fraud or abuse, others reflect missing documentation or administrative errors. For example, a state or contractor may miss a required administrative step, where completing that step would have established the payment was proper. Estimated Fiscal Year (FY) 2026 Improper Payment Rates: Original Medicare: 7.32%, or $33.96 billion, compared to the FY 2025 reported rate of 6.55%, or $28.83 billion. The FY 2026 estimate marks the tenth consecutive year this figure has been below the 10% threshold for compliance established by improper payment statutory requirements. 1 Medicare Part C : 5.68%, or $23.86 billion, compared to the FY 2025 reported rate of 6.09%, or $23.67 billion. Most Part C improper payments were attributable to situations where the Medicare Advantage Organization’s supporting documentation failed to substantiate beneficiary diagnosis data submitted for payment. Medicare Part D : 3.85%, or $5.16 billion, compared to the FY 2025 reported rate of 4%, or $4.23 billion. Most Part D improper payments occurred because plan sponsors failed to provide sufficient documentation to support prescription data used for payment determinations. Medicaid: 7.08%, or $46.84 billion (composed of the past three cycles of approximately 17 states per cycle from reviews in 2024, 2025, and 2026), compared to the FY 2025 reported rate of 6.12%, or $37.39 billion. About 79.41% of the improper payments were the result of insufficient documentation. The Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) : 9.81%, or $2.26 billion (composed of reviews in 2024, 2025, and 2026), compared to the FY 2025 reported rate of 7.05%, or $1.37 billion. About 55.93% of the improper payments were the result of insufficient documentation. The increase in national Medicaid and CHIP improper payment estimates reflects, in part, the effects of unwinding the flexibilities given to states during the COVID-19 public health emergency, such as conducting eligibility redeterminations and provider revalidation requirements, which resumed in April 2023. Advance Payments of the Premium Tax Credit (APTC) program for the Federally-Facilitated Exchange (FFE) for Benefit Year 2024 (Jan. 1 to Dec. 31, 2024): The FY 2026 improper payment rate, for BY 2024 is 0.84% or $830.37 million, compared to the FY 2025, for BY 2023, reported rate of 0.89%, or $657.46 million. The primary cause of improper payments was overpayments due to automated errors (59.24% of improper payments) where most relate to duplicate payment errors, which encapsulates duplicate member and duplicate use of Social Security Number (SSN) errors. The secondary cause of improper payments was overpayments found in manual errors related to failures to properly examine consumer submitted documents. While CMS’ improper payment reporting programs are not designed to measure fraud, the agency is committed to crushing fraud, waste, and abuse throughout its programs and fully expects these efforts to impact improper payment rates going forward. The 2026 Original Medicare and Medicaid/CHIP improper payment measurements are based on claims submitted from July 1, 2024, through June 30, 2025. This timeframe is before many of CMS’ current crushing fraud initiatives were implemented including: Medicare enrollment moratoria for high-risk provider types (including home health agencies and hospices); Large-scale provider enrollment revocations and payment suspensions targeting suspicious billing patterns; Greater use of advanced data analytics to identify high-risk Medicaid providers and coordinate rapid investigations with states and HHS' Office of Inspector General; Development of new data dashboards that give states a Super Intelligence-powered tool to track claims and catch Medicaid outliers before losses occur. To further strengthen stewardship of taxpayer dollars and secure the Medicare Trust Fund, CMS is also advancing a best-in-class commercial claims processing effort, ClaimsCore, that will re-platform Original Medicare claims processing onto a secure, configurable, and modern foundation. CMS estimates it will save millions through this work, not including the additional billions that may be saved through improved program integrity. ClaimsCore is designed to support modern payment integrity controls, faster and more transparent policy execution, and advanced capabilities such as Super Intelligence, while improving operational efficiency and care delivery over time. The impact of these and CMS’ other actions to combat fraud will begin to appear in the improper payment data for FY 2027, with more substantial effects expected in FY 2028. What You Need to Know: The Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019 (Public Law 116- 117) defines significant improper payments as either: Greater than $10 million and over 1.5% of all payments made under that program, or Greater than $100 million. The FY 2026 HHS Agency Financial Report provides the improper payment data for the Original Medicare, Medicare Part C, Medicare Part D, Medicaid, CHIP, and Affordable Care Act Health Insurance Exchange APTC programs. Most improper payments occurred in situations where a reviewer could not determine if a payment was proper because of insufficient documentation from a state, provider, a Medicare Advantage Organization, Part D Sponsor, or Marketplace insurer. Improper payments can result from a variety of circumstances, including: Items or services with no documentation; Items or services with insufficient documentation; Items or services with documentation that does not substantiate the payment; Items or services where the payment was to the right recipient for the right amount, but the payment process did not comply with applicable statutory or regulatory payment requirements; or With respect to Medicaid and CHIP, there is no record of the required verification of an individual’s eligibility factors, such as income. Proper payments occur when there is sufficient documentation to support payment in accordance with the program payment requirements. Two examples of proper payments include: Payments where CMS or the state appropriately maintained documentation of an eligibility verification requirement and appropriately determined eligibility based on program eligibility and payment requirements. Payments where sufficient documentation was provided to support program payment requirements. More information on CMS’ Improper Payments Measurement Programs can be found at: https://www.cms.gov/data-research/monitoring-programs/improper-payment-measurement-programs.
